messages.subject: factor analysis, time varying
parts:
I have a time varying, factor analysis model with a shrinkage parameter that I am estimating.  The model that I have runs, but is very slow.  Any thoughts about how to speed it up? 
The data are a panel with 5 issues(j), 195 individuals, and 16 time periods.  The shrinkage parameter is phi. 

Model is Y_ijt=betat[j,t]_Yijt-1+sigma
beta[j,t]=normal(phi[j,t]*beta[j,t][t-1]+(1-phi1[j,t])*gamma[t],pow(tau[j][1],-2));

To reduce the parameters, I constrained tau to be the same for each issue.

I wasn't sure if there was a way to make the y1,y2,y3,y4,y5 into an array (j,t,n) and if that would speed it up.  I didn't see any factor analysis models that might address this issue in the examples.
Obviously, there are ways to try to tackle the shrinkage parameter with pooling (although it is less clear how to do that with a factor analysis model), but I was hoping I could get this model to work
since it provides a closer fit to the problem I working on.

Thanks,
Greg
Model:
panel1<-"
data {
  int<lower=0> N; ##respondents, 195
  int<lower=0> T; ##time 16
  real y1[N,T]; ##5 meaaures per individual
  real y2[N,T];
  real y3[N,T];
  real y4[N,T];
  real y5[N,T];
}
parameters {
  real beta1[T];
  real beta2[T]; 
  real beta3[T]; 
  real beta4[T]; 
  real beta5[T]; 
  real gamma[T];
 real<lower=0> tau[5];
real phi1[T];
 real phi2[T];
 real phi3[T];
 real phi4[T];
 real phi5[T];
vector<lower=0>[5]sigma;

} 


model
{ 
sigma ~ inv_gamma(.1,0.001);

gamma ~ normal(0,100);

beta1 ~ normal(0,100);
beta2 ~ normal(0,100);
beta3 ~ normal(0,100);
beta4 ~ normal(0,100);
beta5 ~ normal(0,100);
phi1 ~ normal(0,10);
phi2 ~ normal(0,10);
phi3 ~ normal(0,10);
phi4 ~ normal(0,10);
phi5 ~ normal(0,10);

tau ~ inv_gamma(.1,0.01);

for (t in 2:T)  {
beta1[t] ~normal(phi1[t]*beta1[t-1]+(1-phi1[t])*gamma[t],pow(tau[1],-2));
beta2[t] ~normal(phi2[t]*beta2[t-1]+(1-phi2[t])*gamma[t],pow(tau[2],-2));
beta3[t] ~normal(phi3[t]*beta3[t-1]+(1-phi3[t])*gamma[t],pow(tau[3],-2));
beta4[t] ~normal(phi4[t]*beta4[t-1]+(1-phi4[t])*gamma[t],pow(tau[4],-2));
beta5[t] ~normal(phi5[t]*beta5[t-1]+(1-phi5[t])*gamma[t],pow(tau[5],-2));
}

for(n in 1:N){
for (t in 2:T){
real mu1[N,T];
real mu2[N,T];
real mu3[N,T];
real mu4[N,T];
real mu5[N,T];


mu1[n,t]<-beta1[t]*y1[n,t-1];
y1[n,t] ~ normal(mu1[n,t], pow(sigma[1],-2));

mu2[n,t]<-beta2[t]*y2[n,t-1];
y2[n,t] ~ normal(mu2[n,t], pow(sigma[2],-2));

mu3[n,t]<-beta3[t]*y3[n,t-1];
y3[n,t] ~ normal(mu3[n,t], pow(sigma[3],-2));

mu4[n,t]<-beta4[t]*y4[n,t-1];
y4[n,t] ~ normal(mu4[n,t], pow(sigma[4],-2));

mu5[n,t]<-beta5[t]*y5[n,t-1];
y5[n,t] ~ normal(mu5[n,t], pow(sigma[5],-2));

}
}
}
"

messages.author: 743bbacc59f4b25f
messages.subject: Re: factor analysis, time varying
parts:
On Friday, August 2, 2013 9:35:49 AM UTC-4, Greg McAvoy wrote:
I have a time varying, factor analysis model with a shrinkage parameter that I am estimating.  The model that I have runs, but is very slow.  Any thoughts about how to speed it up?

One thing is to not have sampling statements (with the ~) inside a loop with the current version of Stan. Instead, you want to make a temporary mean vector, fill that in a loop, and do one sampling statement outside the loop. This is talked about in the FAQ

https://groups.google.com/d/msg/stan-users/4gv3fNCqSNk/J6ZItL2ZJ-IJ

But it looks like you have used the wrong parameterization for the normal distribution. In Stan, the second parameter is the standard deviation. In BUGS, it is the precision (inverse of the variance). In other words, you have a lot of unnecessary pow(*, -2) calls, although that affects the interpretation a lot more than the speed.

Ben

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] factor analysis, time varying
parts:
On 8/2/13 9:35 AM, Greg McAvoy wrote:
> I have a time varying, factor analysis model with a shrinkage parameter that I am estimating. The model that I have
> runs, but is very slow. Any thoughts about how to speed it up?
> The data are a panel with 5 issues(j), 195 individuals, and 16 time periods. The shrinkage parameter is phi.
>
> Model is Y_ijt=betat[j,t]_Yijt-1+sigma
> beta[j,t]=normal(phi[j,t]*beta[j,t][t-1]+(1-phi1[j,t])*gamma[t],pow(tau[j][1],-2));
>
> To reduce the parameters, I constrained tau to be the same for each issue.

Letting tau vary might not slow things down.

Our normal distribution is parameterized by scale (i.e., standard deviation),
so you almost certainly don't want to be doing pow(tau,-2) anywhere. Maybe
pow(tau,-0.5) if tau is a precision parameter. s
> I wasn't sure if there was a way to make the y1,y2,y3,y4,y5 into an array (j,t,n) and if that would speed it up.

It won't really speed things up, but it should make
the code a lot cleaner.
> didn't see any factor analysis models that might address this issue in the examples.

I've been meaning to add one. We implemented Evan Sandhaus's
MS thesis (he's a grad student here), which was an environment
contimants and source model.

> Obviously, there are ways to try to tackle the shrinkage parameter with pooling (although it is less clear how to do
> that with a factor analysis model), but I was hoping I could get this model to work
> since it provides a closer fit to the problem I working on.
>
> Thanks,
> Greg
> Model:
> panel1<-"
> data {
> int<lower=0> N; ##respondents, 195
> int<lower=0> T; ##time 16
> real y1[N,T]; ##5 meaaures per individual
> real y2[N,T];
> real y3[N,T];
> real y4[N,T];
> real y5[N,T];
> }
> parameters {
> real beta1[T];
> real beta2[T];
> real beta3[T];
> real beta4[T];
> real beta5[T];
> real gamma[T];
> real<lower=0> tau[5];
> real phi1[T];
> real phi2[T];
> real phi3[T];
> real phi4[T];
> real phi5[T];
> vector<lower=0>[5]sigma;
>
> }
>
>
> model
> {
> sigma ~ inv_gamma(.1,0.001);
>
> gamma ~ normal(0,100);
>
> beta1 ~ normal(0,100);
> beta2 ~ normal(0,100);
> beta3 ~ normal(0,100);
> beta4 ~ normal(0,100);
> beta5 ~ normal(0,100);

You probably don't mean to put two priors on each beta, even
though this one's very weak. This is vectorized, so it's
equivalent to:

for (t in 1:T)
beta1[t] ~ normal(0,100)

but I'm assuming you meant

beta1[1] ~ normal(0,100);

just to kick off the time series. Do you expect values as
high as 200 or 300 here or low as -200 or -300 here? If not,
it helps with convergence to use slightly more informative
priors (what Andrew calls "weakly informative").

> phi1 ~ normal(0,10);
> phi2 ~ normal(0,10);
> phi3 ~ normal(0,10);
> phi4 ~ normal(0,10);
> phi5 ~ normal(0,10);

Is the range here right on scale? You could also easily make
this hierarchical if that makes sense.

>
> tau ~ inv_gamma(.1,0.01);
>
> for (t in 2:T) {

> beta1[t] ~normal(phi1[t] * beta1[t-1]
+(1 - phi1[t]) * gamma[t],
pow(tau[1],-2));

The first thing to do is pull the calculation of scale/sd out, assuming
tau is variance (I'm guessing from the inv_gamma() prior --- there's nothing
special about conjugate priors conceptually or computationally in Stan).

for (t in 1:T)
tau_sd[t] <- sqrt(tau[t]);

Andrew also has other suggestions for priors here --- we tend to
use half Cauchy on the scale parameter. And perhaps slightly less
broad priors on beta1 and phi1, unless you really think they might
start out with values like 300 or -20.

The second thing to do for speed would be to vectorize all of these.

real[T-1] alpha1;
for (t in 2:T)

alpha1[t] <- phi1[t] * beta1[t-1] + (1 - phi1[t]) * gamma[t]

beta1 ~ normal(alpha1,tau[1]);


The third thing to do would be to apply the Matt trick.

parameters {
real beta_raw1[T];

transformed parameters {
real beta1[T];
beta1 <- alpha1 + tau[1] * beta1_raw;
...
}
model {
...
beta1_raw ~ normal(0,1);

> beta2[t] ~normal(phi2[t]*beta2[t-1]+(1-phi2[t])*gamma[t],pow(tau[2],-2));
> beta3[t] ~normal(phi3[t]*beta3[t-1]+(1-phi3[t])*gamma[t],pow(tau[3],-2));
> beta4[t] ~normal(phi4[t]*beta4[t-1]+(1-phi4[t])*gamma[t],pow(tau[4],-2));
> beta5[t] ~normal(phi5[t]*beta5[t-1]+(1-phi5[t])*gamma[t],pow(tau[5],-2));
> }
>
> for(n in 1:N){
> for (t in 2:T){
> real mu1[N,T];
> real mu2[N,T];
> real mu3[N,T];
> real mu4[N,T];
> real mu5[N,T];
>
>
> mu1[n,t]<-beta1[t]*y1[n,t-1];
> y1[n,t] ~ normal(mu1[n,t], pow(sigma[1],-2));
>
> mu2[n,t]<-beta2[t]*y2[n,t-1];
> y2[n,t] ~ normal(mu2[n,t], pow(sigma[2],-2));
>
> mu3[n,t]<-beta3[t]*y3[n,t-1];
> y3[n,t] ~ normal(mu3[n,t], pow(sigma[3],-2));
>
> mu4[n,t]<-beta4[t]*y4[n,t-1];
> y4[n,t] ~ normal(mu4[n,t], pow(sigma[4],-2));
>
> mu5[n,t]<-beta5[t]*y5[n,t-1];
> y5[n,t] ~ normal(mu5[n,t], pow(sigma[5],-2));
>
> }
> }
> }
> "

So without the Matt trick or any modification to the priors
(other than assuming that tau and sigma were variances), it'd look like this:

data {
int<lower=0> N; // respondents, N = 195
int<lower=0> T; // time T = 16
real y[5,N,T]; // measures per individual = 5
}
parameters {
real beta[5,T];

real gamma[T];
real<lower=0> tau[5];
real phi[5,T];

vector<lower=0>[5] sigma;
}
model {
sigma ~ inv_gamma(.1,0.001);

tau ~ inv_gamma(.1,0.01);
gamma ~ normal(0,100);
for (k in 1:5)
beta[k,1] ~ normal(0,100);
for (k in 1:5)
phi[k] ~ normal(0,10);
for (k in 1:5) {
real sqrt_tau_k;
sqrt_tau_k <- sqrt(tau[k]);
for (t in 2:T)

beta[k,t] ~ normal(phi[k,t] * beta[k,t-1]
+ (1 - phi[k,t]) * gamma[t],
sqrt_tau_k);
}
for (k in 1:5) {
real sqrt_sigma_k;
sqrt_sigma_k <- sqrt(sigma[k]);

for(n in 1:N)
for (t in 2:T)

y[k,n,t] ~ normal(beta[k,t] * y[k,n,t-1],
sqrt_sigma_k);
}
}

To apply the Matt trick on this loop isn't any harder:

beta[k,t] ~ normal(phi[k,t] * beta[k,t-1]
+ (1 - phi[k,t]) * gamma[t],
sqrt_tau_k);

use:

beta_raw[k,t] ~ normal(0,1);

and

beta[k,t] <- phi[k,t] * beta[k,t-1] + (1 - phi[k,t]) * gamma[t]
+ beta_raw[k,t] * sqrt_tau_k;

But as you can see, each of these optimizations makes the model
a bit harder to read.

- Bob

I have been out of town and just got back to this.  The program (revised by Bob) runs beautifully now, faster than I had ever imagined!  Even with the sampling in the loop, Stan optimized this quickly. I did let the tau (variances) vary across time and that didn't pose any problems for optimization.  I haven't tried the Matt trick yet but hope to soon.  

I will echo the sentiments that researchers have previously posted here...the support you are providing for Stan is remarkable!

Best,
Greg
